title: AI answers run on a library nobody is paying for
notes: Emphasis markup: [[word]] renders in the accent yellow. Use on two slides per set at most.

lines: AI answers run on a library.
The meters only count the answers.
Here's what nobody is paying for:

slides.headline: The deals stopped moving.
slides.deck: At a Digiday town hall in London, one publishing executive said talks with AI companies have all but stopped. Meanwhile, People Inc. sees tens of thousands of bots a day. It blocks all but 38.

slides.headline: Pay per [[crawl]] is over. Now it's pay per [[use]].
slides.deck: Cloudflare switched in July. Google and Microsoft are testing the same idea.

slides.text: That's how much of what ChatGPT retrieves makes it into its final answers, per AirOps research covering more than 548,000 pages. The other 85% still shaped the answer.

slides.headline: Uncited doesn't mean worthless.
slides.deck: Say an agent reads three sources on a company's layoffs: the original report, a wire story and some financial background. It uses one, maybe two. The money follows the same path.

slides.headline: A tenth of a cent per article.
slides.deck: Exa charges $1 for every 1,000 pages of full text. Parallel's Extract is $1 per 1,000 URLs. That is what a page of your reporting is worth to a data broker.

slides.quote: “They do not create things, they resell things.”
slides.deck: Jonathan Roberts, chief innovation officer at People Inc., on the AI data brokers. His company blocks all but 38 of the bots that hit its sites.

slides.lead: Pete Pachal's fix, borrowed from Spotify:
items: A nominal, flat fee just for being in the index.
Real money as your content delivers actual value.
More for unique reporting nobody else has.

slides.text: Pete Pachal's bottom line: a meter that counts only [[answers]] will always undervalue the [[library]], and the library is what makes those answers any good.

slides.question: Would you create new content for a market that pays a tenth of a cent an article?

At the Financial Times, one trial account tried to access about a million articles in eight hours, from 700,000 IP addresses. The brokers that resell that kind of haul charge about a dollar per thousand pages.
Pete Pachal's column this week on why pay-per-use meters shortchange the library behind every AI answer, and the Spotify-style fix he proposes.
Someone has to pay for the pantry, not just what lands on the plate. Who should it be?
